Rule. Hold this rule for Adapter: Wrap a type you do not own so the caller keeps the interface it already has. Say it before you pick a tool from Design patterns.

Why it matters. Interviewers on the Design patterns track listen for whether you can name the idea adapter and refuse the common wrong pick. The summary is the force: Wrap a type you do not own so the caller keeps the interface it already has. If you cannot restate it, you will drift into product names or trivia.

SAMPLE example. SAMPLE: a prompt lands that fits Adapter. You restate the force in one sentence — Wrap a type you do not own so the caller keeps the interface it already has. — then show a tiny walkthrough that would fail if you ignored that force. You label the SAMPLE answer with the cost or the tradeoff, not with a brand name.

When to use. Use Adapter when the prompt's access pattern or force matches the summary above, when a prior slug in its after-list is already in hand, and when saying the rule changes which next step you take.

When to refuse. Refuse Adapter when a simpler tool already covers the force, when a prerequisite in after is still missing, or when applying it would invent a mechanism the track never taught. Prefer naming the missing slug over bluffing.
